n: Ezekiel begins a series of acted-out prophecies—living object lessons. First he draws Jerusalem on a clay brick, the kind used for writing and building in Babylon.

f.g: A soft clay brick; Babylonians often drew maps and plans on such tablets.

n: Like a child with toy soldiers, he builds a miniature siege around the drawing: siege wall, ramp, army camps, and battering rams. The exiles watching would grasp that Jerusalem was doomed.

f.g: Build a siege ramp of earth up to the city wall.
Heavy beams used to break city gates and walls.

n: An iron griddle placed between Ezekiel and the brick represents an unbreakable barrier: God himself has set his face against the city, and prayer will not break through.

f.g: A flat iron plate or griddle used for baking.

f.w: This shall be a sign to the house of Israel

n: Ezekiel must lie on his left side to “bear” the iniquity of the northern kingdom of Israel—symbolically carrying their guilt and its punishment.

f.g: To carry the burden and consequence of sin, as the scapegoat did symbolically.

n: Each day stands for a year—390 days for Israel’s long years of sin. Scholars debate exactly which period the 390 years measure.

f.g: The ancient Greek translation reads 190; the meaning of the number is uncertain.

n: Then he lies on his right side for 40 days, one day for each year of Judah’s iniquity. Forty recalls Israel’s 40 years of wandering in the wilderness.

f.w: I have appointed thee each day for a year

n: With arm bared like a warrior ready to strike, he faces the model siege and prophesies against Jerusalem.

f.g: A sign of action and power.

n: God will bind him so he cannot roll over until the siege days are complete. He probably lay in this posture for part of each day, as he also had to prepare food.
He must mix many kinds of grain and legumes into one bread—a famine loaf made from whatever scraps can be found, since no single grain is available in quantity.

f.g: Spelt, a coarse kind of wheat.
Mixing grains was unusual and suggests desperation.

n: His daily bread ration is only about twenty shekels—roughly 8 ounces (230 grams)—a starvation diet.
His water ration is about two-thirds of a quart (0.6 liter) per day—another sign of siege conditions.

f.w: the sixth part of an hin

n: He is told to bake the bread over human dung as fuel, publicly. This shocks a priest, because it would make the food ritually unclean.

f.g: Dried animal dung was common fuel in the region; human waste was considered defiling.

n: God explains the sign: in exile, Israel will be forced to eat unclean food among the Gentiles, cut off from the purity laws of their homeland.
Ezekiel protests honestly. As a priest he has always kept the dietary laws and never eaten forbidden or dead animals.

f.w: that which dieth of itself, or is torn in pieces

f.g: Sacrificial meat left too long, which became forbidden.

n: God mercifully allows him to use cow dung instead—a common fuel. The Lord listens to the sincere concerns of his servants.

f.g: Dried cattle dung, widely used as cooking fuel.

n: God explains: he will “break the staff of bread” in Jerusalem. People will weigh out food anxiously and drink rationed water in horror.

f.g: Bread as the support of life; to break it means famine.

n: Lacking food and water, they will stare at one another in shock and waste away because of their sins—just as Lamentations later describes.
